Derived via Western European languages from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατία (aristokratía). Compare Russian аристокра́тия (aristokrátija), Belarusian арыстакра́тыя (arystakrátyja).

From Ancient Greek βουλιμία (boulimía, “ravenous hunger”), from βοῦς (boûs, “cow, ox”) + λῑμός (līmós, “hunger”). Compare Russian булими́я (bulimíja).

From Ancient Greek θεολόγος (theológos). Also analyzable as тео(ло́гія) (teo(lóhija)) + -лог (-loh).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θεραπευτής (therapeutḗs).
From Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). Compare Russian термоме́трия (termométrija), Belarusian тэрмаме́трыя (termamjétryja), Polish termometria.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θῆτα (thêta).

Ultimately from Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē) + -κρατία (-kratía). With техно- (texno-) prefix. Compare Russian технокра́тия (texnokrátija), Belarusian тэхнакра́тыя (texnakrátyja), Polish technokracja.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē, “art”). With -ло́г (-lóh) ending.

Ultimately from Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē, “art”), with -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). Compare Russian техноло́гия (texnológija), Belarusian тэхнало́гія (texnalóhija), Polish technologia.
Possibly a back-formation from те́хніка (téxnika), from Ancient Greek τεχνικός (tekhnikós). Cognate with Russian те́хник (téxnik), Belarusian тэ́хнік (téxnik).
From Old East Slavic тигръ (tigrŭ), ultimately from Ancient Greek τίγρις (tígris).
From Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), compare also the colloquial meaning of Greek τύπος (týpos, “man, guy”) and German Typ (“guy, bloke”).

From Old East Slavic ктиторъ (ktitorŭ), from Ancient Greek κτίτωρ (ktítōr, “founder”), an incorrect spelling of κτήτωρ (ktḗtōr) influenced by κτίζω (ktízō, “I found, build, establish”). Cognates include Russian ти́тар (títar), кти́тор (ktítor, “church warden”).

Ultimately from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón), with -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). Compare Russian токсиколо́гия (toksikológija), Belarusian таксікало́гія (taksikalóhija), Polish toksykologia.

parole.significato: topaz (a rare silicate mineral made of aluminum and fluorine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τόπαζος (tópazos) via French topaze and Latin topazus.
From Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + γράφω (gráphō, “I write”).

Derived via Western European languages from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place, location”) and ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). Compare Russian топо́ним (topónim), Belarusian тапо́нім (tapónim), Polish toponim.

parole.significato: trauma, injury (any serious injury to the body, often resulting from violence or an accident)
parole.testo: Derived via Western European languages from Ancient Greek τραῦμᾰ (traûmă).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek τρίπτυχος (tríptukhos, “consisting of three layers, threefold”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θρόμβωσις (thrómbōsis).
From Latin thunnus + -е́ць (-écʹ), from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos). Compare Russian and Belarusian туне́ц.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek τῐᾱ́ρᾱ (tĭā́rā). Compare Russian тиа́ра (tiára), Belarusian тыя́ра (tyjára).
From Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ, “Pharaoh”), from Biblical Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (parʿōh), from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ (“palace, pharaoh”, literally “pr (“house”) + ꜥꜣ (“great, big”)”).

Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek φάρμακον (phármakon) + -λογία (-logía), with -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending. Compare Russian фармаколо́гия (farmakológija), Belarusian фармакало́гія (farmakalóhija), Polish farmakologia.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek φαρμακευτής (pharmakeutḗs), later form of φαρμακεύς (pharmakeús, “sorcerer, poisoner; druggist, apothecary”).
Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek φαρμακευτική (pharmakeutikḗ).
Derived via Western European languages from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon).
From Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice, sound”) + -λογία (-logía). With -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending. Compare Russian фоноло́гия (fonológija), Belarusian фанало́гія (fanalóhija), Polish fonologia.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek φωτο- (phōto-, combining form of φῶς (phôs, “light”)).

Derived via Western European languages (English photogenic, French photogénique), ultimately from Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός (phôs, phōtós) + -γενής (-genḗs). With -і́чний (-íčnyj) suffix. Compare Russian фотогени́чный (fotogeníčnyj), Belarusian фотагені́чны (fotahjeníčny), Polish fotogeniczny.
Derived via Western European languages from Ancient Greek φωτός (phōtós), genitive singular of φῶς (phôs, “light”) (fōs) and γράφω (gráphō, “I write”).
Derived via Western European languages (English photography, French photographie) from Ancient Greek φωτός (phōtós, “of light”, genitive) and γράφω (gráphō, “I write”).

From Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “speech”) + -λογία (-logía). With -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending. Compare Russian фразеоло́гия (frazeológija), Belarusian фразеало́гія (frazjealóhija), Polish frazeologia.
From Ancient Greek φθορά (phthorá, “destruction, deterioration”), because of the corrosive action of hydrofluoric acid.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φεῖ (pheî).
Derived via Western European languages from Ancient Greek φιλάνθρωπος (philánthrōpos). Compare Russian филантро́п (filantróp).

From Ancient Greek φιλολογία (philología), with -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). Compare Russian филоло́гия (filológija), Belarusian філало́гія (filalóhija), Polish filologia.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos). Compare Russian фило́соф (filósof), Belarusian філо́саф (filósaf), Polish filozof.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía). Compare Russian филосо́фия (filosófija), Belarusian філасо́фія (filasófija), Polish filozofia.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek φίμωσις (phímōsis).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek θυμίαμα (thumíama).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χαλεπά (khalepá), χαλεπός (khalepós). Cognate with Belarusian халепа (xaljepa).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos, “vast chasm, void”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma, “grace, favour, gift”).
From Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma), with -и́чний (-ýčnyj) ending. Compare Russian харизмати́чный (xarizmatíčnyj), Belarusian харызматы́чны (xaryzmatýčny), Polish charyzmatyczny.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek χώρᾱ (khṓrā, “location, place”) and ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
From Христо́с (Xrystós) + -ло́гія (-lóhija), from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós) and -λογία (-logía). Compare Russian христоло́гия (xristológija), Polish chrystologia.
From Ancient Greek χθών (khthṓn, “ground, soil”) + -і́чний (-íčnyj).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χεῖ (kheî).

parole.significato: chiton (a loose woolen tunic worn by men and women in Ancient Greece)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek χιτών (khitṓn).

Internationalism ultimately from Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”) + φρήν (phrḗn, “mind, heart, diaphragm”). Compare Russian шизофре́ник (šizofrénik), Belarusian шызафрэ́нік (šyzafrénik), Polish schizofrenik.
From щит (ščyt, “shield”) + -о- (-o-) + поді́бний (podíbnyj, “similar”), a calque of Ancient Greek θῠρεοειδής (thŭreoeidḗs, “shield-shaped”). Compare Belarusian шчытападо́бны (ščytapadóbny).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós). Compare Russian иудаи́зм (iudaízm), Belarusian іўдаі́зм (iwdaízm), Polish judaizm.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).
From Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos)

parole.significato: evangelical (a member of an evangelical church)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs, “bringer of good news”), from εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō, “to evangelize”), from εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + ἀγγέλλω (angéllō, “to announce”). With -і́ст (-íst) suffix.

parole.significato: eunuch (a castrated male servant of a harem)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).
From Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos). Derived with the suffix -ей (-ej).
From Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer, supervisor”). Doublet of бі́скуп (bískup). Compare Russian епи́скоп (jepískop), Belarusian епі́скап (jepískap).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós).
Inherited from Old East Slavic идолъ (idolŭ), from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὗ ψιλόν (hû psilón).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Ἰουδά (Ioudá) + -ιος (-ios). Ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yəhūḏā(h), “Judah”). Derived with the suffix -ей (-ej).
From Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía). Compare Russian иера́рхия (ijerárxija), Belarusian іера́рхія (ijerárxija), Polish hierarchia.

Of unclear origin. The Russian cognate ахине́я (axinéja) is thought to derive either from dialectal Russian охи́нить (oxínitʹ, “to scold”) (related to хинь (xinʹ, “nonsense”) and хи́нить (xínitʹ, “to abuse”)) or from a seminarian usage of the word афинейский (afinejskij) in the sense of 'falsely lea

parole.significato: basilisk, basilisk lizard (tree-dwelling lizard of the genus Basiliscus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian василіскъ (vasylisk), from either Old East Slavic василискъ (vasiliskŭ) or Old Church Slavonic василискъ (vasiliskŭ), from Ancient Greek βασιλίσκος (basilískos). Compare Belarusian васілі́ск (vasilísk), Russian васили́ск (vasilísk).
Derived via either Polish horyzont or German Horizont from Latin horīzōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn).
Borrowed from either German Jod or directly from French iode, from Ancient Greek ἰοειδής (ioeidḗs, “violet”).

parole.significato: department/school/college in a university or institute; chair.
parole.testo: From Middle Ukrainian каѳедра (kafedra), катедра (katedra), ultimately either from Latin cathedra or Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).

Borrowed from either German Obelisk or French obélisque, from Latin obeliscus, from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), from ὀβελός (obelós, “spit, skewer”). Compare Russian обели́ск (obelísk), Belarusian абелі́ск (abjelísk).

From Old Polish *rakovina, ultimately related to Ancient Greek κάρυον (káruon, “nut, shell”) or from Latin arca (“chest, coffer”), via Old East Slavic and Proto-Slavic. Shares roots with Ukrainian ра́к (rák, “crayfish”).
